title: 1 · I want, I can
intro: We'll build real sentences from two little engine words — no memorising lists. Take your time, say each answer out loud before you reveal it.

steps.teach: "Ich wott" = I want. Add a verb straight onto it. "cho" = to come (English "come", with the k→ch shift).
"Ich cha" = I can.
"schlofe" = to sleep (English "sleep", p→f).
To make a question, just flip the two words — like English "I can" → "can I".
steps.hint: an n slips in to join them: Cha-n-i

steps.teach: "nöd" = not. It comes right after the verb.

title: 2 · I must, help, go
intro: Same engine, new words. Everything from lesson 1 still applies — we're just adding pieces.

steps.teach: "Ich mues" = I must / I have to. "goh" = to go.
"hälfe" = to help (English "help", p→f again).
"Chasch" = can you, "mer" = me.

title: 3 · I have, I am
intro: Two more everyday engines — "I have" and "I am" — the ones you'll reach for constantly.

steps.teach: "Ich ha" = I have. "Ziit" = time (note the ii — English "tide/time").
"Hunger" = hunger; Swiss say "I have hunger" for "I'm hungry".
"Ich bi" = I am. "müed" = tired.

title: 4 · you, we, he, she
intro: So far everything's been "I". Now the other people — the verb ending shifts a little, but the engine words stay the same.

steps.teach: "du" = you. With "du", the verb takes -sch: come → chunnsch.
steps.hint: you can drop "du" — the ending already says "you"

steps.teach: "Häsch" = you have.
"er" = he. With "er", come → chunnt.
"si" = she — same verb form as he.
"mir" = we. With "mir", come → chömed.

title: 5 · where, what, when
intro: Little question words open up whole conversations. Put the question word first, then flip in the verb.

steps.teach: "Wo" = where. "bisch" = you are.
"Was" = what. "machsch" = you do / you're doing.
"Wänn" = when.
"Wie" = how.

title: 6 · and, but, eat, drink
intro: Now join sentences together. "und" = and, "aber" = but — plus two verbs you'll reach for every day.

steps.teach: "ässe" = to eat (English "eat", with the t→s shift).
"und" = and. "trinke" = to drink (English "drink", d→t).
steps.prompt: I want to eat and drink

steps.teach: "aber" = but.
steps.prompt: I'm hungry, but I have no time
steps.answer: Ich ha Hunger, aber ich ha kei Ziit.
steps.hint: I'm hungry = Ich ha Hunger · no time = kei Ziit

title: 7 · Yesterday, and what you did
intro: The past in Züritüütsch is one pattern, and it's the same shape as English "I have done". Once you have it, every verb you already know works in the past too.

steps.teach: The past is built with "ha" (have) plus the verb at the end — exactly like English "I have eaten". "gässe" = eaten (English "eat", with t→ss).
And that's also how you say the plain past. Swiss barely uses a simple past tense — "Ich ha gässe" covers both "I have eaten" and "I ate".
Most of these past forms start with g-. "gseit" = said.
"gmacht" = made, done.
steps.hint: you already know häsch = you have

steps.teach: Verbs of *going* take "sii" (to be) instead of "ha" — like older English "I am come". "ggange" = gone.
"cho" (to come) is the same: it takes sii. And its past form is just "cho" again.

steps.prompt: We ate and then we went
steps.answer: Mir händ gässe und denn sind mir ggange.
steps.hint: händ = we have, sind = we are

title: 8 · Me, you, him — the little words
intro: These are the words that make a sentence about somebody. Swiss has two sets — one for the person doing something *to*, one for the person it's done *for* — and the difference is worth feeling rather than memorising.

steps.teach: "mich" = me, when I'm the one being acted on.
"mer" = to me, for me — when something is given or said to me.
Feel the difference: hälfe (to help) takes the *to-me* one, because in Swiss you help *to* somebody.
steps.hint: not mich — hälfe always takes mer

steps.teach: "dich" = you (acted on), "der" = to you.
"ihm" = to him, "ihre" = to her.
"üs" = us, or to us.

title: 9 · One, two, many — and the -li trick
intro: Plurals in Swiss are less regular than English, so we won't pretend otherwise. But there's one ending that turns *anything* into a small friendly version, and it's the most Swiss thing in the language.

steps.teach: Add "-li" to make something small, or just to be fond of it. English has this as -let or -y: piglet, doggy. "Bier" → a little beer.
It works on almost anything. "Hund" = dog.
And it's how Swiss makes things sound friendly rather than literally small. "Sätzli" = a few little sentences — what you do in this app.
Anything with -li takes "es" (it), whatever the original word was.
Now plain numbers. "zwei" = two, and the noun often just doesn't change.
"vill" = a lot, much, many — one word for all of them.
steps.hint: Lüt = people, related to German Leute

title: 10 · Asking for things without being rude
intro: Almost everything polite in Swiss is built from one shape: the would-form. Learn it once and every request gets softer.

steps.teach: "Ich hätt" = I would have. It's the polite engine — the softened version of "Ich ha".
Add "gärn" (gladly) and you have the standard way to order anything at all.
"Chönnti" = could I. Softer than "Chan ich".
"Wär" = would be. Useful for suggestions.
"Wärs müglich" = would it be possible. The most polite thing in the language.
And the magic word that makes almost anything acceptable: "exgüsi" = excuse me, sorry. French again.
steps.prompt: Excuse me, could I ask something?

title: 11 · Because, but, although
intro: These are the words that turn two sentences into one thought. There's one thing to watch: some of them push the verb to the end, and Swiss does this exactly where German does.

steps.teach: "aber" = but, and it changes nothing about the word order. The easy one.
steps.prompt: I want to come, but I have no time
steps.answer: Ich wott cho, aber ich ha kei Ziit.

steps.teach: "wil" = because — and this one sends the verb to the *end* of its half.
Put it together and feel the verb slide back.
steps.prompt: I can't come because I have no time
steps.answer: Ich cha nöd cho, wil ich kei Ziit ha.

steps.teach: "dass" = that, and it does the same thing.
steps.answer: Ich glaub, dass es guet isch.

steps.teach: "öb" = whether, if. Also sends the verb back.
steps.prompt: I don't know whether he's coming
steps.answer: Ich weiss nöd, öb er chunnt.

steps.teach: "obwohl" = although.

steps.prompt: I'm coming although I have no time
steps.answer: Ich chume, obwohl ich kei Ziit ha.

title: 12 · Sounding Swiss rather than correct
intro: A last set: the small words that carry tone. None of them translate cleanly, and they're the difference between a correct sentence and one a Zürcher would actually say.

steps.teach: "scho" = already, but mostly it's reassurance. "Das gaht scho" = that'll be fine.
"halt" = just, simply — a shrug in one syllable. It means "that's how it is".
"ja" dropped mid-sentence means "as you know" — the I-told-you-so particle.
"mal" softens a request into something casual.
"eifach" = simply. Use it when you want someone to stop overthinking.
"oder?" on the end turns any statement into a check — like English "...right?". Zürich says it constantly.

title: 13 · He, she, and the words that follow
intro: Swiss marks gender in more places than English does — the article, the possessive, the job word. That sounds like more to learn, but it's really three small patterns, and each one works on everything.

steps.teach: "Er" = he, "si" = she. The verb doesn't change between them, which makes this the easy half.
Same verb, other person.
Now the article. "de" goes with a man, "d" with a woman, "s" with a child. The word's gender is carried by the article, so learn them together.
And the masculine one.
"min" = my, before a masculine word. Add "-i" before a feminine one.
That -i is the whole change.
Somebody else's: "sin" = his, "iri" = her. Same shape, different owner.
Job words take "-in" to make them feminine. One ending, hundreds of words: Lehrer → Lehrerin, Arzt → Ärztin.
steps.hint: no "a" needed — Swiss drops it before a job

steps.teach: Careful with the vowel: Arzt softens to Ärztin.
Last one. Giving something to somebody: "ihm" to a man, "ihre" to a woman.
